anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, datatypes, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing scans or non-covering look-ups that inflate I/O and lock footprints.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions compete for incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or tables, resulting in blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput and trigger rollbacks or timeouts.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Underlying storage devices are saturated in bandwidth, IOPS, or latency, so each physical read or write stalls, independent of database configuration.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits compounded symptoms: queries that already perform full scans or many non-selective index probes generate large volumes of physical I/O against an over-subscribed storage layer, pushing device queues to their limits and inflating I/O latency. Slower I/O prolongs statement execution, leaving locks held open longer and expanding the window for conflicting transactions to collide. This magnifies lock-wait chains, deadlock frequency, connection-pool exhaustion, and application timeouts. Meanwhile, blocked sessions accumulate, creating bursty "thundering-herd" releases that further spike I/O demand when locks are freed, perpetuating the saturation cycle. Overall, CPU usage remains uneven, with threads oscillating between runnable yet waiting on I/O and lock events, while business throughput degrades sharply and variability in response times escalates.

Causal interaction: Poor schema and missing or non-optimal indexes force the engine to touch far more data than necessary, increasing both the number of pages locked and the volume of read/write requests. The bloated lock scope raises the probability of conflicts, while the excess I/O pushes the storage subsystem into sustained saturation. Elevated I/O latency slows down every lock-protected operation, keeping locks active longer and intensifying contention; heightened contention in turn clusters wake-ups and retries, generating I/O bursts that exacerbate storage overload. Thus, each root cause amplifies the others, driving a feedback loop that degrades transactional performance far more severely than any single anomaly alone.

entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with logical data inconsistency, structural corruption, uniqueness conflicts, or referential-integrity rules being violated by the workload or storage state.
entry.solution_guidance: Validate data consistency, inspect constraints and index integrity, and check whether data-cleaning, repair, or workload correction is required before retrying.
